transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, what finally made me come in is this business of checking things, and I know that sounds small when I say it out loud, but it’s become... it’s become hard to just go about my day. I’ll check the same boxes, or lists I’ve made, or drawers in the condo, and then I’ll have to check them again before I can move on. And the frustrating part is, I know perfectly well I already looked. I can remember looking. But somehow that doesn’t settle it.

My wife will be standing there waiting for me to just leave it alone, and I want to, I really do, but I get caught up in making sure one more time. Then one more after that. It’s not that anything dramatic happens, exactly, but it slows everything down and makes me feel rather foolish and stuck. That’s really why I’m here.
Besides checking things, do you find yourself having other repetitive thoughts or feeling like you have to perform certain actions a specific way?

Yes, I do, though I’m not sure if it’s exactly the same sort of thing. It’s more these thoughts that get stuck in my head, nagging at me. For example, I’ll start thinking I may have thrown away something important from my old teaching files — some paper or note or record that I might need, even though realistically I know I probably don’t need it anymore. Or I’ll worry that I put a tool in the wrong box, and then later I won’t be able to find it when I need it.

And the thing is, I can tell myself, “Now, come on, that’s unlikely,” or “You would remember if you’d thrown that out,” but it doesn’t quite land. The thought comes back again, and then I feel like I can’t really settle down or move on until I’ve somehow reassured myself about it. It’s not always loud, if that makes sense, but it’s persistent. It sort of keeps tapping me on the shoulder.
When you have these recurring thoughts, do they lead you to do certain things—like checking, organizing, or repeating actions—to try to feel better or prevent something bad from happening?

Yes, that’s exactly what happens, I suppose. The thought will come up, and then I feel I have to do something with it, not just let it sit there. So I’ll go back and check the same box, or the same list, or a drawer in the condo, even if I’ve already opened it and looked inside.

And I know I’ve already looked — that’s the maddening part. It isn’t that I’ve forgotten in the usual sense. I can remember standing there and checking it. But there’s still this feeling of, “Well, maybe just make sure once more,” and then once more after that. It’s as if I can’t quite move on to the next thing until I’ve done it enough times, though I couldn’t tell you what “enough” is.

My wife will be waiting for me, sometimes literally standing there ready to go, and I can see that she wants me to just leave it alone. I want to leave it alone too. But I get pulled back into checking, and it’s embarrassing, really, because part of me is watching myself do it and thinking, “You already did this.” But I still feel I have to check before I can settle.
Do these thoughts and checking behaviors cause you significant distress or interfere with your daily life, such as taking up a lot of time or affecting your work or relationships?

Yes, it does interfere, though I’d call it more wearing and time-consuming than catastrophic, if that distinction makes sense. The biggest example lately is unpacking the condo. That should have been a fairly ordinary job — boxes, shelves, sorting things into drawers — but it has stretched on much longer than it had any right to, because I keep stopping to verify what’s in a box, or where I put something, or whether I put it in the correct place.

And then because I haven’t “finished” that, or because it doesn’t feel finished enough, I put off other things. I do some library tutoring preparation, or at least I’m supposed to, and I’ll find myself not starting it because I feel I have to settle the condo things first. Same with hobbies — things I used to just sit down and do, I’ll delay because there’s this sense that I can’t move on until I’m sure enough about whatever I was checking.

So yes, it’s affecting my days. It’s not ruining everything, but it eats up time and makes ordinary tasks feel much heavier than they should.
Do you ever feel that you need to perform certain actions a specific number of times, in a certain way, or until it feels 'just right,' even if it's not directly related to what you're worried about?

Yes… I think the “until it feels right” part fits more than a particular number. I don’t usually say to myself, “I have to do this three times,” or anything as clear as that. It’s more that I check the same boxes, or the same list, or the condo drawers again and again until I can somehow let myself move on.

And that’s what really brought me in, honestly. I’ll know perfectly well that I already looked. I can remember opening the drawer, seeing what was inside, closing it. But then I’ll be halfway to the door, or my wife will be standing there waiting for me to just leave it be, and I get this pull to go back and make sure one more time. Not because there’s some new reason, exactly. Just because it doesn’t feel settled.

It’s embarrassing, because I know it looks unnecessary, and I know it is unnecessary in a practical sense. But in the moment, leaving it unchecked feels harder than going back and doing it again.

Do you ever feel the need to arrange things in a certain way, make sure things are perfectly aligned, or repeat actions until they feel exactly right, even if it’s not about checking for safety or preventing something bad?

Not so much the arranging or lining things up, no. I don’t really have a thing where objects have to be perfectly straight or symmetrical, at least not that I’ve noticed.

For me it’s much more the repeating until I can move on. What brought me in is that I keep finding myself checking the same boxes, the same lists, the same condo drawers over and over. I know perfectly well I already looked — I can remember looking — but it still doesn’t feel settled. My wife might be standing there waiting for me, and I know she wants me to just leave it be, and I want that too. But I’ll still feel pulled back to check it again, almost like I need that last look before I can go on to the next thing.
Do you ever have thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or welcome—thoughts that feel intrusive or upsetting, even if you’re not always acting on them?

Yes, I do. They’re not dramatic thoughts, exactly, but they’re intrusive in the sense that I don’t invite them and I can’t seem to just dismiss them when they show up.

A common one is this nagging thought that I may have thrown away something important from my old teaching files — some paper or note or folder that I’ll need later, even if I haven’t needed it in years. Or I’ll think maybe I put a tool in the wrong box while unpacking, and then the thought just sits there and bothers me. I’ll tell myself, “Well, that’s probably not true,” or “If it were really important, I’d know,” but it doesn’t quite take. It comes back around again, and then I have trouble settling down and moving on to whatever I was trying to do next.

It’s upsetting mostly because it feels unreasonable, and I know that. I can argue with it logically, but it still keeps tapping me on the shoulder, so to speak.
When you have these intrusive thoughts, do you feel driven to do something — like checking, repeating, or reassuring yourself — to try to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yes, that’s exactly the pattern, I think. The thought comes in, and then I feel like I have to do something to quiet it down — usually checking.

What brought me in is that I keep checking the same boxes, the same lists, and the drawers at the condo over and over before I can move on. And the odd thing is, I do know I already looked. I’m not confused about it. I can remember looking in the drawer, or going through the list, or checking the box, and still it feels like there’s this unfinished feeling, like I can’t quite trust it unless I look again.

It’s not that my wife hasn’t been patient, but she’ll be standing there waiting for me to just leave it alone, and I can see how unnecessary it looks from the outside. I know perfectly well that I already checked. But in the moment, checking again feels like the only way to get that anxious feeling to settle enough so I can move on.
Do you ever find it difficult to throw things away or feel a need to keep items longer than you think you reasonably should, even if they don’t seem useful to others?

I’m not entirely sure how to answer that, because I don’t think of myself as someone who keeps things just for the sake of keeping them. I mean, I have old papers and household things like anyone my age would, and sometimes I’ll hesitate before throwing something out, especially if it seems like it might have some future use. But I wouldn’t say I have piles of useless things that I can’t part with, or that rooms are taken over by belongings, if that’s what you mean.

With teaching materials, for example, there are things I’ve kept longer than someone else might think is necessary, but in my mind they had some possible value or history attached to them. So I don’t know if that counts. It doesn’t feel like collecting or hoarding to me. It’s more that I can get stuck wondering whether something might turn out to matter later, and then I’m slower to toss it. But as a general need to keep everything, no, I haven’t really noticed that.
Do you ever find it hard to get rid of items, even ones that seem useless or have no real value, because the idea of throwing them away feels unsettling or causes you distress?

I don’t think so, not in that way. I mean, I can hesitate with things, especially if I get into that frame of mind of, “Well, what if I need this later?” But if something is truly useless to me, or has no real value that I can see, I don’t usually feel distressed in the sense of being unable to let it go.

Sometimes I may take longer than I should deciding, because I’ll sort of review what it is, where it came from, whether it belongs with other papers or household items, that sort of thing. My wife would probably say I can make too much of a small decision. But it’s not that the object itself feels impossible to part with. It’s more the uncertainty around whether I’m making the right decision.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I have a strong distress about throwing away useless things just because they’re being thrown away. It’s more that I can get bogged down in deciding whether they really are useless.

Do you ever feel that you have to perform certain mental acts—like counting, praying, or going over something in your mind—a certain way or a certain number of times to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce your anxiety?

Not so much counting or praying, no. It’s more… going back over it in my head only seems to happen around the checking. Like with the boxes or the lists or the drawers at the condo, I’ll know I already looked, and I can even picture myself having looked. But then my mind sort of replays it and says, “Are you sure? Did you really see it properly?” And then I feel pushed to check again.

It isn’t usually a set number, like three times or seven times. It’s more that I don’t feel done until it feels settled, if that makes sense. My wife will be waiting for me, and I’ll know she wants me to just leave it be, and part of me agrees with her completely. But the anxious feeling doesn’t really let go until I’ve checked again, even though I know perfectly well I already did.

Do you ever find it difficult to discard items, even ones that seem to have no real value, because you feel a strong need to save them or because it causes you significant distress to throw them away?

I don’t think that’s really a big issue for me, no. I mean, I may pause over things longer than is sensible, especially papers or old household items where I’m thinking, “Well, maybe this could be useful,” or “Maybe I should check what this is before tossing it.” But it’s not usually because I feel some powerful need to save it, or because throwing it away feels intolerable.

If something really has no value and I can identify it as trash, I can get rid of it. I might take a little too long deciding, and sometimes I’ll second-guess whether I’ve sorted it correctly, but I don’t feel deeply attached to the item itself. It’s more that I like to be sure I’m not making a mistake.

So, in the way you’re asking it—significant distress about discarding, even useless things—I’d say no, I haven’t noticed that in myself.

Do you ever find yourself repeating words, phrases, or numbers in your head, or feel the need to do something mentally a certain way to reduce anxiety, even if it's not connected to checking or organizing physical objects?

Not really in a separate way, no. I mean, I can’t think of myself sitting there repeating a word or a number in my head to make something feel safe. The thing that keeps happening—the thing that really brought me in—is still tied to checking.

It’s those boxes, or the lists, or the drawers at the condo. I’ll look once, and I’ll know I looked. Then I’ll be ready to move on, or at least I’ll think I’m ready, and then this doubt comes back in: “Did I actually check that properly?” And before I can leave it alone, I end up checking again. Sometimes my wife is right there waiting for me, and I know she wants me to just let it be, and honestly I want to let it be too. But I don’t quite feel able to move on until I’ve gone back over it.

So I wouldn’t say it’s words or numbers in my head, exactly. It’s more that mental uncertainty that pushes me back into checking the same things, even when I know perfectly well I already did.
Do you ever feel that you have to check things even when there’s no real reason to worry about them, just to make sure your mind feels at ease?

Yes… yes, that’s exactly it, really. I’ll know there’s no sensible reason to be worried. I mean, with the boxes or the lists or those drawers at the condo, I can look at them and know, on one level, that I already checked. Sometimes I can even remember the moment of checking, like I can picture my hand opening the drawer or my eyes going down the list.

But then there’s this little unsettled feeling that comes right back, almost like my mind won’t accept it as finished. It’s not that I truly believe something terrible is sitting there waiting to happen every time. It’s more that I don’t feel able to move on until I’ve checked again, just to quiet that doubt.

And my wife will be there waiting for me, and I can tell she wants me to leave it alone, and honestly I want to leave it alone too. I’m not enjoying it. I know it looks unnecessary. But I end up going back over the same things anyway, because otherwise my mind keeps nagging at me that maybe I missed something, even though I know perfectly well I already looked.

When you have these intrusive thoughts that make you want to check things again, do you feel like they’re something you have to fight against, or do they feel like something you should just give in to? And when you check again, does it feel more like something you’re doing to stop yourself from feeling anxious, rather than something you enjoy doing?

Yes, I’d say it feels much more like something I’m resisting, or at least trying to resist, than something I think is a good idea. I don’t sit there thinking, “Oh, this is useful, I should do this again.” It’s more like I’ve already checked the box, or the list, or the drawer at the condo, and I know I checked it — I really do know it — but then I get this uncomfortable doubt that sort of keeps tugging at me.

And I try to move on. Especially if my wife is there waiting, which she often is, and I can feel that she wants me to just leave it alone and go. I want to do that too. But I’ll be standing there thinking, “Just walk away, you already looked,” and then almost immediately another part of me says, “But what if you didn’t look carefully enough?” or “What if you missed something?” So I end up going back and checking again.

It’s not enjoyable. Not at all. It’s frustrating, honestly, because it makes me feel a bit foolish. I’m not getting pleasure from opening the same drawer again or going over the same list again. It’s just that checking seems to quiet that anxious, unsettled feeling for a little while, enough that I can move on — though sometimes only after doing it more than once.
Do you ever feel that things need to be arranged a certain way, or that something has to be done exactly right, even if it’s not about checking for safety or making sure you didn’t make a mistake?

I don’t think so, no. At least not in the way you’re describing it. I’m trying to think of examples, like lining things up or needing things to be symmetrical, or having to do something in a very exact way just because it feels wrong otherwise, and that doesn’t really sound like me.

I mean, I like things to be reasonably tidy, I suppose, but I don’t have that feeling that, say, objects on a table have to be in a certain position or that I have to repeat an action until it feels perfectly done. If something is crooked or out of place, I might notice it, but it doesn’t usually bother me in that particular way.

The main thing for me is still more that doubt after I’ve checked something. It’s not so much that it has to be arranged perfectly or done in some special order. It’s more… did I really do it, did I miss something, that sort of thing. But outside of that, no, I haven’t noticed a need for things to be “just right” for its own sake.

Have you ever had thoughts that something is not quite right unless it feels balanced or exact, even if you can’t explain why, or thoughts that keep coming up that aren’t about checking but still bother you?

Not so much the balanced or exact feeling, no. I don’t usually get bothered because something isn’t symmetrical or lined up in some special way.

But I do get other thoughts that keep coming back, and they’re not always exactly the same as just checking a door or a drawer. A lot of it is this nagging idea that I may have gotten rid of something important, especially from my old teaching files. I’ll think, “What if I threw away a paper or a note or some record that I really should have kept?” And I can tell myself, “Well, if it was important, you probably wouldn’t have thrown it away,” or “You sorted those things carefully,” but the thought doesn’t always let go.

It’s similar with tools, too. If I’ve been putting things into boxes, I’ll start wondering if I put a needed tool in the wrong box, or if I mixed something up and won’t be able to find it later. And again, I know it’s probably unlikely. I know that. But the thought comes back anyway, and then it’s hard to feel settled. It just sits there in the background, bothering me until I feel like I have to make sure somehow.
Do these checking behaviors or the thoughts that come with them take up more than an hour of your day?

I don’t think it’s more than an hour most days, no. It can feel like it takes up more space in my head than it probably does on the clock, if that makes sense.

What brought me in is that I’ll be trying to leave or finish up, and I find myself checking the same boxes, the same lists, or the condo drawers over and over before I can move on. I know perfectly well I already looked — that’s the maddening part — and often my wife is standing there waiting for me to just leave it alone. So it may only be a few minutes here and there, but those minutes feel very drawn out because I’m arguing with myself the whole time.

If I added it all up, I’d say it’s usually under an hour in a day, but it’s enough that it’s bothering me and holding us up.
Do you ever have intrusive thoughts or feel the need to check things related to germs, dirt, or contamination, such as worrying that something is dirty or might make you sick?

No, not really. I mean, I wash my hands like anyone else, and if something is obviously dirty I’d clean it or avoid touching it, but I don’t have that kind of fear that germs are everywhere or that I’m going to get sick from touching ordinary things.

I don’t find myself repeatedly washing or checking whether something is contaminated. That hasn’t been one of the things that gets stuck in my mind. If I’m concerned about something being dirty, it’s usually for a normal reason — like if it actually looks dirty — and then I just deal with it and move on. It doesn’t have that same pull or nagging feeling to it.

Same with hobbies — things I used to just sit down and do, I’ll delay because there’s this sense that I can’t move on until I’m sure enough about whatever I was checking.

So yes, it’s affecting my days. It’s not ruining everything, but it eats up time and makes ordinary tasks feel much heavier than they should.

target_item.reason: The question asks about repetitive arranging, aligning, or repeating actions until they feel 'just right,' which is most directly about compulsive behaviors.

patient.answer:
Not so much the arranging or lining things up, no. I don’t really have a thing where objects have to be perfectly straight or symmetrical, at least not that I’ve noticed.

For me it’s much more the repeating until I can move on. What brought me in is that I keep finding myself checking the same boxes, the same lists, the same condo drawers over and over. I know perfectly well I already looked — I can remember looking — but it still doesn’t feel settled. My wife might be standing there waiting for me, and I know she wants me to just leave it be, and I want that too. But I’ll still feel pulled back to check it again, almost like I need that last look before I can go on to the next thing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences intrusive, unwanted thoughts that cause distress, which is a key feature of obsessive-compulsive disorder and helps differentiate between the current candidate diagnoses.
doctor.question: Do you ever have thoughts that come into your mind that you don’t want or welcome—thoughts that feel intrusive or upsetting, even if you’re not always acting on them?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: I keep getting these nagging thoughts that I may have thrown away something important from my old teaching files or put a needed tool in the wrong box, and even when I tell myself it's unlikely, the thought comes back and makes it hard to settle.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about unwanted, intrusive thoughts that come into the patient's mind, which corresponds most directly to obsessions.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do. They’re not dramatic thoughts, exactly, but they’re intrusive in the sense that I don’t invite them and I can’t seem to just dismiss them when they show up.

A common one is this nagging thought that I may have thrown away something important from my old teaching files — some paper or note or folder that I’ll need later, even if I haven’t needed it in years. Or I’ll think maybe I put a tool in the wrong box while unpacking, and then the thought just sits there and bothers me. I’ll tell myself, “Well, that’s probably not true,” or “If it were really important, I’d know,” but it doesn’t quite take. It comes back around again, and then I have trouble settling down and moving on to whatever I was trying to do next.

It’s upsetting mostly because it feels unreasonable, and I know that. I can argue with it logically, but it still keeps tapping me on the shoulder, so to speak.

inference.note: The patient continues to describe symptoms consistent with recurrent intrusive thoughts and repetitive checking behaviors that cause significant distress and impairment in daily functioning. The absence of a need for things to be arranged in a specific way or symmetry concerns makes F42.3 and F42.4 less likely. The symptoms are not better explained by another disorder, and the clinical picture remains consistent with OCD subtypes related to checking and rumination. The differential remains unchanged.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsions aimed at reducing anxiety or preventing a feared event, which is key to differentiating OCD from other anxiety disorders.
doctor.question: When you have these intrusive thoughts, do you feel driven to do something — like checking, repeating, or reassuring yourself — to try to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that I find myself checking the same boxes, lists, and condo drawers over and over before I can move on, even though I know perfectly well I already looked and my wife is waiting for me to just leave it be.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether intrusive thoughts lead to driven behaviors like checking, repeating, or reassurance to reduce anxiety or prevent harm, which directly matches compulsions.

patient.answer:
Yes, that’s exactly the pattern, I think. The thought comes in, and then I feel like I have to do something to quiet it down — usually checking.

What brought me in is that I keep checking the same boxes, the same lists, and the drawers at the condo over and over before I can move on. And the odd thing is, I do know I already looked. I’m not confused about it. I can remember looking in the drawer, or going through the list, or checking the box, and still it feels like there’s this unfinished feeling, like I can’t quite trust it unless I look again.

It’s not that my wife hasn’t been patient, but she’ll be standing there waiting for me to just leave it alone, and I can see how unnecessary it looks from the outside. I know perfectly well that I already checked. But in the moment, checking again feels like the only way to get that anxious feeling to settle enough so I can move on.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of hoarding or difficulty discarding items, which would help differentiate between OCD subtypes or other disorders.
doctor.question: Do you ever find it difficult to throw things away or feel a need to keep items longer than you think you reasonably should, even if they don’t seem useful to others?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about difficulty discarding or saving items, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not entirely sure how to answer that, because I don’t think of myself as someone who keeps things just for the sake of keeping them. I mean, I have old papers and household things like anyone my age would, and sometimes I’ll hesitate before throwing something out, especially if it seems like it might have some future use. But I wouldn’t say I have piles of useless things that I can’t part with, or that rooms are taken over by belongings, if that’s what you mean.

With teaching materials, for example, there are things I’ve kept longer than someone else might think is necessary, but in my mind they had some possible value or history attached to them. So I don’t know if that counts. It doesn’t feel like collecting or hoarding to me. It’s more that I can get stuck wondering whether something might turn out to matter later, and then I’m slower to toss it. But as a general need to keep everything, no, I haven’t really noticed that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of hoarding disorder, which is relevant for differentiating F42.8 (other obsessive-compulsive disorders) from F42.2 (obsessive-compulsive disorder, with hoarding) and F42.1 (obsessive-compulsive disorder, with compulsive rituals).
doctor.question: Do you ever find it hard to get rid of items, even ones that seem useless or have no real value, because the idea of throwing them away feels unsettling or causes you distress?

target_item.reason: The question is directly about hoarding-type difficulty discarding items because throwing them away causes distress, which is not covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not in that way. I mean, I can hesitate with things, especially if I get into that frame of mind of, “Well, what if I need this later?” But if something is truly useless to me, or has no real value that I can see, I don’t usually feel distressed in the sense of being unable to let it go.

Sometimes I may take longer than I should deciding, because I’ll sort of review what it is, where it came from, whether it belongs with other papers or household items, that sort of thing. My wife would probably say I can make too much of a small decision. But it’s not that the object itself feels impossible to part with. It’s more the uncertainty around whether I’m making the right decision.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I have a strong distress about throwing away useless things just because they’re being thrown away. It’s more that I can get bogged down in deciding whether they really are useless.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences compulsions in the form of repetitive behaviors or mental acts that he feels driven to perform in response to an obsession, which is key in differentiating OCD subtypes and confirming the diagnosis.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel that you have to perform certain mental acts—like counting, praying, or going over something in your mind—a certain way or a certain number of times to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce your anxiety?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that I find myself checking the same boxes, lists, and condo drawers over and over before I can move on, even though I know perfectly well I already looked and my wife is waiting for me to just leave it be.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about repetitive mental acts performed in a specific way or number of times to reduce anxiety or prevent something bad, which directly corresponds to compulsions.

patient.answer:
Not so much counting or praying, no. It’s more… going back over it in my head only seems to happen around the checking. Like with the boxes or the lists or the drawers at the condo, I’ll know I already looked, and I can even picture myself having looked. But then my mind sort of replays it and says, “Are you sure? Did you really see it properly?” And then I feel pushed to check again.

It isn’t usually a set number, like three times or seven times. It’s more that I don’t feel done until it feels settled, if that makes sense. My wife will be waiting for me, and I’ll know she wants me to just leave it be, and part of me agrees with her completely. But the anxious feeling doesn’t really let go until I’ve checked again, even though I know perfectly well I already did.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of hoarding disorder, specifically difficulty discarding items due to perceived need to save them and distress associated with discarding them, which is important in differentiating between OCD and hoarding disorder.
doctor.question: Do you ever find it difficult to discard items, even ones that seem to have no real value, because you feel a strong need to save them or because it causes you significant distress to throw them away?

target_item.reason: The question is about difficulty discarding items due to a strong need to save them or distress about throwing them away, which relates to hoarding-like symptoms. The provided symptom profile covers obsessions, compulsive checking, and functional impairment, but not hoarding or saving behaviors.

patient.answer:
I don’t think that’s really a big issue for me, no. I mean, I may pause over things longer than is sensible, especially papers or old household items where I’m thinking, “Well, maybe this could be useful,” or “Maybe I should check what this is before tossing it.” But it’s not usually because I feel some powerful need to save it, or because throwing it away feels intolerable.

If something really has no value and I can identify it as trash, I can get rid of it. I might take a little too long deciding, and sometimes I’ll second-guess whether I’ve sorted it correctly, but I don’t feel deeply attached to the item itself. It’s more that I like to be sure I’m not making a mistake.

So, in the way you’re asking it—significant distress about discarding, even useless things—I’d say no, I haven’t noticed that in myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsions that are not connected to their checking behaviors, such as repeating words or phrases, counting, or other mental rituals, which could help differentiate between OCD subtypes.
doctor.question: Do you ever find yourself repeating words, phrases, or numbers in your head, or feel the need to do something mentally a certain way to reduce anxiety, even if it's not connected to checking or organizing physical objects?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that I find myself checking the same boxes, lists, and condo drawers over and over before I can move on, even though I know perfectly well I already looked and my wife is waiting for me to just leave it be.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about mental rituals or repetitive mental acts done to reduce anxiety, which falls under compulsions.

patient.answer:
Not really in a separate way, no. I mean, I can’t think of myself sitting there repeating a word or a number in my head to make something feel safe. The thing that keeps happening—the thing that really brought me in—is still tied to checking.

It’s those boxes, or the lists, or the drawers at the condo. I’ll look once, and I’ll know I looked. Then I’ll be ready to move on, or at least I’ll think I’m ready, and then this doubt comes back in: “Did I actually check that properly?” And before I can leave it alone, I end up checking again. Sometimes my wife is right there waiting for me, and I know she wants me to just let it be, and honestly I want to let it be too. But I don’t quite feel able to move on until I’ve gone back over it.

So I wouldn’t say it’s words or numbers in my head, exactly. It’s more that mental uncertainty that pushes me back into checking the same things, even when I know perfectly well I already did.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences compulsions that are aimed at preventing or reducing anxiety or distress, but that are not clearly connected to a realistic concern or event.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel that you have to check things even when there’s no real reason to worry about them, just to make sure your mind feels at ease?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that I find myself checking the same boxes, lists, and condo drawers over and over before I can move on, even though I know perfectly well I already looked and my wife is waiting for me to just leave it be.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about repeated checking done despite no real reason, in order to relieve anxiety or feel mentally at ease, which directly matches compulsions.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, that’s exactly it, really. I’ll know there’s no sensible reason to be worried. I mean, with the boxes or the lists or those drawers at the condo, I can look at them and know, on one level, that I already checked. Sometimes I can even remember the moment of checking, like I can picture my hand opening the drawer or my eyes going down the list.

But then there’s this little unsettled feeling that comes right back, almost like my mind won’t accept it as finished. It’s not that I truly believe something terrible is sitting there waiting to happen every time. It’s more that I don’t feel able to move on until I’ve checked again, just to quiet that doubt.

And my wife will be there waiting for me, and I can tell she wants me to leave it alone, and honestly I want to leave it alone too. I’m not enjoying it. I know it looks unnecessary. But I end up going back over the same things anyway, because otherwise my mind keeps nagging at me that maybe I missed something, even though I know perfectly well I already looked.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences obsessions that are resisted and recognized as excessive or unreasonable, and whether compulsions are aimed at preventing anxiety or distress rather than providing pleasure, to differentiate between OCD subtypes and support diagnosis.
doctor.question: When you have these intrusive thoughts that make you want to check things again, do you feel like they’re something you have to fight against, or do they feel like something you should just give in to? And when you check again, does it feel more like something you’re doing to stop yourself from feeling anxious, rather than something you enjoy doing?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that I find myself checking the same boxes, lists, and condo drawers over and over before I can move on, even though I know perfectly well I already looked and my wife is waiting for me to just leave it be.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the repeated checking is something the patient gives in to in order to reduce anxiety rather than something enjoyable, which most directly concerns compulsions.

patient.answer:
Yes, I’d say it feels much more like something I’m resisting, or at least trying to resist, than something I think is a good idea. I don’t sit there thinking, “Oh, this is useful, I should do this again.” It’s more like I’ve already checked the box, or the list, or the drawer at the condo, and I know I checked it — I really do know it — but then I get this uncomfortable doubt that sort of keeps tugging at me.

And I try to move on. Especially if my wife is there waiting, which she often is, and I can feel that she wants me to just leave it alone and go. I want to do that too. But I’ll be standing there thinking, “Just walk away, you already looked,” and then almost immediately another part of me says, “But what if you didn’t look carefully enough?” or “What if you missed something?” So I end up going back and checking again.

It’s not enjoyable. Not at all. It’s frustrating, honestly, because it makes me feel a bit foolish. I’m not getting pleasure from opening the same drawer again or going over the same list again. It’s just that checking seems to quiet that anxious, unsettled feeling for a little while, enough that I can move on — though sometimes only after doing it more than once.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences obsessions or compulsions related to symmetry, exactness, or a need for things to feel 'just right', beyond checking behaviors, to help differentiate between OCD subtypes (F42.2, F42.1, F42.8).
doctor.question: Do you ever feel that things need to be arranged a certain way, or that something has to be done exactly right, even if it’s not about checking for safety or making sure you didn’t make a mistake?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symmetry/ordering or needing things done exactly right apart from checking, but the provided symptom profile only covers intrusive thoughts about misplaced/discarded items, checking compulsions, and functional impairment from checking; it does not describe arranging or exactness symptoms.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, no. At least not in the way you’re describing it. I’m trying to think of examples, like lining things up or needing things to be symmetrical, or having to do something in a very exact way just because it feels wrong otherwise, and that doesn’t really sound like me.

I mean, I like things to be reasonably tidy, I suppose, but I don’t have that feeling that, say, objects on a table have to be in a certain position or that I have to repeat an action until it feels perfectly done. If something is crooked or out of place, I might notice it, but it doesn’t usually bother me in that particular way.

The main thing for me is still more that doubt after I’ve checked something. It’s not so much that it has to be arranged perfectly or done in some special order. It’s more… did I really do it, did I miss something, that sort of thing. But outside of that, no, I haven’t noticed a need for things to be “just right” for its own sake.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences obsessions related to symmetry, exactness, or intrusive thoughts unrelated to checking, which would help distinguish between OCD subtypes and other diagnoses.
doctor.question: Have you ever had thoughts that something is not quite right unless it feels balanced or exact, even if you can’t explain why, or thoughts that keep coming up that aren’t about checking but still bother you?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: I keep getting these nagging thoughts that I may have thrown away something important from my old teaching files or put a needed tool in the wrong box, and even when I tell myself it's unlikely, the thought comes back and makes it hard to settle.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about intrusive, recurring bothersome thoughts beyond checking, including 'not quite right' thoughts; this most directly maps to obsessions rather than the checking behavior itself.

patient.answer:
Not so much the balanced or exact feeling, no. I don’t usually get bothered because something isn’t symmetrical or lined up in some special way.

But I do get other thoughts that keep coming back, and they’re not always exactly the same as just checking a door or a drawer. A lot of it is this nagging idea that I may have gotten rid of something important, especially from my old teaching files. I’ll think, “What if I threw away a paper or a note or some record that I really should have kept?” And I can tell myself, “Well, if it was important, you probably wouldn’t have thrown it away,” or “You sorted those things carefully,” but the thought doesn’t always let go.

It’s similar with tools, too. If I’ve been putting things into boxes, I’ll start wondering if I put a needed tool in the wrong box, or if I mixed something up and won’t be able to find it later. And again, I know it’s probably unlikely. I know that. But the thought comes back anyway, and then it’s hard to feel settled. It just sits there in the background, bothering me until I feel like I have to make sure somehow.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences obsessions or compulsions that are time-consuming (taking more than one hour per day) to confirm criteria for OCD subtypes.
doctor.question: Do these checking behaviors or the thoughts that come with them take up more than an hour of your day?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is that I find myself checking the same boxes, lists, and condo drawers over and over before I can move on, even though I know perfectly well I already looked and my wife is waiting for me to just leave it be.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how much time the repeated checking behaviors take up, which most directly relates to the compulsive checking.

patient.answer:
I don’t think it’s more than an hour most days, no. It can feel like it takes up more space in my head than it probably does on the clock, if that makes sense.

What brought me in is that I’ll be trying to leave or finish up, and I find myself checking the same boxes, the same lists, or the condo drawers over and over before I can move on. I know perfectly well I already looked — that’s the maddening part — and often my wife is standing there waiting for me to just leave it alone. So it may only be a few minutes here and there, but those minutes feel very drawn out because I’m arguing with myself the whole time.

If I added it all up, I’d say it’s usually under an hour in a day, but it’s enough that it’s bothering me and holding us up.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences intrusive thoughts or checking behaviors related to contamination or germs, which would help distinguish between the remaining OCD subtypes.
doctor.question: Do you ever have intrusive thoughts or feel the need to check things related to germs, dirt, or contamination, such as worrying that something is dirty or might make you sick?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about contamination-related intrusive thoughts or checking around germs, dirt, or illness, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile focused on checking boxes, lists, drawers, teaching files, and tools.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, I wash my hands like anyone else, and if something is obviously dirty I’d clean it or avoid touching it, but I don’t have that kind of fear that germs are everywhere or that I’m going to get sick from touching ordinary things.

I don’t find myself repeatedly washing or checking whether something is contaminated. That hasn’t been one of the things that gets stuck in my mind. If I’m concerned about something being dirty, it’s usually for a normal reason — like if it actually looks dirty — and then I just deal with it and move on. It doesn’t have that same pull or nagging feeling to it.
